name: Igbo-Ukwu culture
info: The Igbo-Ukwu culture of south-eastern Nigeria, known from a shrine, a burial and a cache first dated to the 9th century CE, cast the region’s earliest known bronzes and traded for beads from beyond the Sahara.

facts.homeland: Igbo-Ukwu, a town in Anambra State, south-eastern Nigeria, on a ridge between the Aghomili and Obizi rivers; sites Igbo Isaiah (a shrine), Igbo Richard (a burial chamber) and Igbo Jonah (a cache)
facts.period: Dated to the 9th century CE by Thurstan Shaw’s radiocarbon dates (1970); newer dates from Igbo Isaiah (2022) fall in the 10th–13th centuries, suggesting the sites were in use for several centuries
facts.known: lost-wax bronzes with fine surface detail, among them ritual vessels, pendants, crowns, breastplates, staff ornaments and fly-whisk handles; a rich burial with regalia; about 165,000 glass, carnelian and stone beads; bast and raffia textiles
facts.sources: chance finds by Isaiah Anozie (1938); excavations by Thurstan Shaw (1959–1964) and new fieldwork (2019, 2021); radiocarbon and AMS dating; lead isotope and alloy analysis; chemical study of the beads; microscopy of the textiles

t: Igbo-Ukwu is a town in south-eastern Nigeria whose three excavated sites, a shrine, a burial chamber and a cache, held more than 700 objects of copper, bronze and iron.
Its smiths cast bronzes of such fine detail that experts first doubted they were local; analysis showed that most of the metal came from mines about 100 kilometres away.
Glass beads from as far as Mesopotamia, Iran and Egypt show that Igbo-Ukwu was tied into long-distance trade centuries before Europeans reached the coast.
dyk: Isaiah Anozie, who found the first bronzes while digging in his compound in 1938, did not know what they were: he gave some to friends and neighbours and used some of the vessels to water his goats.
ev: Iron is smelted at Lejja in the Nsukka region, about 100 kilometres east of Igbo-Ukwu
Bronzes, beads and a rich burial are placed at Igbo-Ukwu, according to the first radiocarbon dates
Isaiah Anozie finds bronzes while digging beside his home
The district officer J. O. Field hands the objects he had bought to the Nigerian Department of Antiquities
Thurstan Shaw excavates Igbo Isaiah, Igbo Richard and Igbo Jonah
Shaw publishes radiocarbon dates placing the sites in the 9th century
New radiocarbon dates from Igbo Isaiah fall between the 10th and 13th centuries

sections.origins:
The Igbo-Ukwu culture is an archaeologists’ name for the people who left three rich deposits in what is now the town of Igbo-Ukwu, “Great Igbo”, in Anambra State in south-eastern Nigeria. The town stands about 366 metres above sea level on a sandstone ridge with little groundwater, between the Aghomili River to the east and the Obizi River to the west. Metalworking in the region was far older: furnaces and slag from iron smelting have been dated to 2000 BCE at Lejja and 750 BCE at Opi, both in the Nsukka region about 100 kilometres to the east.

The first finds were made in 1938 by Isaiah Anozie while digging in his compound. J. O. Field, the British district officer, bought many of them, published them, and in 1946 handed them to the Nigerian Department of Antiquities; Kenneth Murray collected more in 1954. From 1959 to 1964 the archaeologist Thurstan Shaw excavated three areas: Igbo Isaiah around the first find, Igbo Richard and Igbo Jonah.

Shaw’s radiocarbon dates, published in 1970, placed the sites in the 9th century, around 850 CE. Newer dates from Igbo Isaiah, published by Daraojimba and colleagues in 2022, fall between the 10th and 13th centuries, and a textile from the same site was dated to about 1027–1180. These results suggest that Igbo-Ukwu may have been used over several centuries, and that some objects may be younger than once thought, though all of them come well before European contact with the coast.
sections.society:
The finds suggest an economy based on farming and trade. Excavations west of Igbo Richard in 2019 and 2021 yielded pottery, bronze, copper and iron objects, iron slag, chalk, bone and palm kernel, and the earlier digs found iron swords, spearheads and razors. Igbo Jonah, the largest excavated area at 19 by 11 metres, produced the least material: its pits had been deliberately backfilled, and it yielded ritual pottery, charcoal, animal bones and some bronzes.

Igbo Richard was a burial chamber holding the remains of several people, beaded wristlets and anklets, and a wooden stool associated with a single skeleton, possibly that of a priest-king; one body was adorned in what appears to be regalia. One of the bronzes is a small pendant in the shape of a chief’s head with ichi scarification marks on the face.

The town of Igbo-Ukwu is described as the capital of the Kingdom of Nri from the 8th or 9th century, and the sites are associated with the Nri-Igbo, though how the deposits relate to that kingdom is not set out in detail. The finds also overturned a colonial-era view that such craft could not come from an acephalous, or egalitarian, society such as that of the Igbo.
sections.beliefs:
The three sites are read as a shrine (Igbo Isaiah), a burial chamber (Igbo Richard) and a cache (Igbo Jonah), and many of the bronzes are ritual vessels. From them archaeologists infer that by the 9th century the people of Igbo-Ukwu had a complex religious system. The burial at Igbo Richard, with its stool and what appears to be regalia, is read by some as that of a priest-king, but this too is interpretation.

The textiles found at Igbo Isaiah have been thought to hold religious or spiritual meaning, but the ethnographic and archaeological evidence for the meaning of bark-fibre cloth in the forest zone is thin, so this remains speculation. Much about the beliefs behind the objects is still unknown.
sections.arts:
The excavations recovered more than 700 high-quality objects of copper, bronze and iron, about 165,000 beads of glass, carnelian and stone, pottery, textiles and ivory. The bronzes were made by lost-wax casting, probably with latex rather than beeswax, which may explain their fine, filigree surface detail. The smiths did not use wire making, soldering or riveting, which suggests a tradition that developed on its own; small insects that seem to have landed on the surface were cast in one piece with the vessel. Complex objects were made in stages and joined by brazing or by casting linking sections, techniques not known elsewhere.

The alloy is unusual, with a high silver content unlike that of Europe, the Mediterranean or other African bronze centres. About 85–90% of the ore came from old mines at Abakaliki, about 100 kilometres away, with a small share from a second source not yet identified; lead isotopes point to possible sources in North Africa. The Grove Encyclopedia of Materials and Techniques in Art calls the bronzes “among the most inventive and technically accomplished bronzes ever made”, and Hugh Honour and John Fleming describe a water pot in a mesh of cast rope as “a virtuoso feat of cire perdue (lost wax) casting”.

The textiles were woven from Ficus bark fibre and raffia palm, with yarn 0.3–0.4 millimetres thick, an old weaving tradition of the Nigerian forest zone that cotton and wool have almost wholly replaced.
sections.exchange:
The beads show long-distance trade. An analysis of 138 of them found that the most common type was soda-lime glass made with plant ash, probably from glass produced in Mesopotamia and eastern Iran and carried along an eastern Niger corridor by the 9th or 10th century. Some glass and carnelian beads have been traced to the workshops of Fustat in Old Cairo. Other glass types have no known source yet, and Susan McIntosh argues that the possibility of trade across the Sahara needs more research.

Igbo-Ukwu is described as the centre of a trade system linking it with Gao on the bend of the Niger and, through Gao, with Egypt and North Africa. Its people traded with other African peoples as far as the Nile valley, while most of their metal came from the Abakaliki mines nearby.
sections.legacy:
The sources do not say how the Igbo-Ukwu culture ended. Its bronzes stand centuries before the other known bronzes of the region, and their quality first led scholars to imagine that they were made after contact with Europeans. Isotope analysis and radiocarbon dating proved them local and far older, and with that they undid the colonial-era assumption that such work could only come from places in touch with Europe. Denis Williams called them “an exquisite explosion without antecedent or issue”, and Frank Willett compared their standard with that of Benvenuto Cellini five centuries later.

Five objects from Isaiah Anozie’s first finds are in the British Museum: a small staff, a ram’s head, a large manilla, a crescent-shaped vessel and the pendant of a chief’s head. After a memorial for Thurstan Shaw in 2014, the Igwe of Igbo-Ukwu, Martin E. Ezeh, allowed new fieldwork, coordinated by Pamela Jane Smith Shaw in 2019 and 2021, which aims to widen the record of the ancient settlement in time and space.

summary: The Igbo-Ukwu culture is known from three sites in a town of south-eastern Nigeria: a shrine, a burial chamber and a cache, first dated to the 9th century CE and possibly used for several centuries. Its smiths cast intricate lost-wax bronzes from nearby ores, and its people traded for beads that came from as far as Egypt, Mesopotamia and Iran. The finds overturned colonial assumptions about early African art.
references: Ehret, C. (2002) The Civilizations of Africa: A History to 1800. James Currey.
notes: Thin material: the two articles give only one full reference (Ehret 2002). Shaw's 1970 dates, Daraojimba et al. 2022 and McIntosh et al. 2022 are named in the text without titles, so they are not listed.

Dates: kept 850–1050 (circa). The first radiocarbon dates give the 9th century (850 CE), but the newer dates from Igbo Isaiah (Daraojimba et al. 2022: 10th–13th centuries) and the AMS date of a textile (1027–1180) suggest use over several centuries; the editor may wish to move the end to c. 1200. The articles also say the Igbo Richard burial's relation to the other two sites is unresolved.

Kingdom of Nri: only the Igbo-Ukwu town article links the two ('capital of the Kingdom of Nri beginning in the 8th or 9th century CE'; sites 'associated with the Nri-Igbo'). I kept to that and said the relation is not set out in detail.

The archaeology article says the Fustat beads prove trade 'to Byzantine-era Egypt'; Fustat was founded after the Arab conquest, so I left out 'Byzantine-era'. The bead study separately points to Mesopotamian and Iranian glass; both are given.
Excavation years vary between the articles (1959 and 1964; 1959–1964; 1960–1964); I used 1959–1964.
